name: Shutter Island
blurb: Scorsese's 1954-set thriller about a marshal hunting a missing patient on an asylum island
title: Shutter Island Explained: Plot Summary and Ending
description: Shutter Island (2010) explained: who is who, the full plot from the ferry to the lighthouse, the twist, and what Teddy's last question means.
h1: Shutter Island Explained: Plot Summary, Characters and Ending
answer: Shutter Island is a 2010 psychological thriller directed by Martin Scorsese, based on Dennis Lehane's 2003 novel, with Leonardo DiCaprio and Mark Ruffalo. In 1954, U.S. Marshal Teddy Daniels and his new partner Chuck Aule take a ferry to Ashecliffe Hospital, an institution for the criminally insane on an island in Boston Harbor. A patient who drowned her three children has vanished from a locked room, and the staff seem unwilling to help. As a storm cuts the island off, Teddy, haunted by the war and by his dead wife, starts to suspect the hospital is hiding something far bigger.

body: Beginning. In 1954 Teddy Daniels and Chuck Aule arrive at Ashecliffe to look for Rachel Solando, who disappeared barefoot from a locked cell. Dr. Cawley is polite but will not hand over staff records, and Rachel's own psychiatrist, Dr. Lester Sheehan, has conveniently left for a holiday. Teddy suffers migraines and vivid flashbacks: liberating the Dachau camp as a soldier, and his wife Dolores, who died in a fire. He tells Chuck the real reason he took the case: the man who set that fire, Andrew Laeddis, is supposedly a patient here, and Teddy suspects Ashecliffe performs illegal experiments on its inmates.

Middle. A hurricane strikes and the marshals are stuck on the island. Rachel turns up unharmed, but she confuses Teddy with her husband. Teddy finds a note reading 'the law of 4' and 'who is 67?', and becomes convinced there is a hidden 67th patient. During the storm he slips into Ward C and finds George Noyce, a former patient who knows Teddy by sight. Noyce says the doctors are experimenting on people, that lobotomies are carried out in the island's lighthouse, and that Chuck cannot be trusted.

Climbing the cliffs toward the lighthouse, Teddy and Chuck are separated. Teddy thinks he sees Chuck's body on the rocks below, climbs down, and finds a cave where a woman says she is the real Rachel Solando. She claims she was a psychiatrist on the staff who discovered mind-control experiments and was committed to silence her. She warns Teddy that the doctors will use his war trauma to declare him insane and keep him, and that the pills and cigarettes he has been given are drugging him. Back at the hospital, Cawley tells Teddy that he arrived on the island alone; there is no partner named Chuck.

End. Teddy overpowers Naehring, makes his way into the lighthouse and climbs to the top, expecting an operating theatre. Instead he finds Cawley sitting at a desk. Cawley tells him the truth: Teddy is Andrew Laeddis, a patient at Ashecliffe for two years. Edward Daniels and Rachel Solando are anagrams of Andrew Laeddis and Dolores Chanal. Andrew's wife Dolores was mentally ill; after she set fire to their apartment he moved the family to a lake house without getting her treatment, and there she drowned their three children. Andrew shot her. Unable to live with it, he invented the heroic marshal Teddy Daniels. Chuck enters: he is Dr. Sheehan, Andrew's psychiatrist. The whole investigation was a role-play the staff allowed so that Andrew could act out his fantasy and reach its end. His migraines come from withdrawal from the drug he had been taking. Shown photographs and the facts of the drownings, Andrew remembers and collapses. When he wakes he tells Cawley the story himself, and Cawley warns that they reached this point once before, nine months earlier, and he slipped back. If it happens again, the board will order a lobotomy.

In the last scene, some time later, Andrew sits on the hospital grounds with Sheehan and calls him Chuck, saying they need to get off the island. Sheehan gives Cawley a small shake of the head, and orderlies come forward to take Andrew for the lobotomy. Before he goes, Andrew asks Sheehan whether it would be worse to live as a monster or to die as a good man. Sheehan, startled, calls after him by the name Teddy; Andrew does not react and walks off calmly with the orderlies. The film ends on a shot of the lighthouse. The operation itself is never shown.

Everything up to the lighthouse is settled: Andrew killed Dolores after she drowned their children, and the marshal story was his delusion. What is debated is the final scene. There are two main readings.

ol: He has relapsed. Andrew has fallen back into being Teddy, the treatment has failed, and the question is a brief flicker of awareness that passes immediately. Dennis Lehane, who wrote the novel, has said in interviews that he sees it this way: a momentary flash of sanity, nothing more. In the book, which does not contain the 'monster or good man' line, the relapse is clearer.

He is pretending. Andrew is lucid and remembers everything, but he chooses to act out the Teddy persona so that he will be lobotomized, because losing his mind is easier than living as the man who failed his children. The new line, added for the film, is the main evidence: it only makes sense from someone who knows what he did. Sheehan's reaction suggests he hears it that way too.

body: Scorsese leaves the choice to the viewer. Either way the film's point is the same: Andrew's guilt is unbearable, and the 'good man' version of himself is the story he cannot let go of.

ul: Guilt and denial: Andrew builds an entire false world, with a villain to hunt, so that he never has to face his own failure to protect his children.
Unreliable perception: the film is shown through Teddy's eyes, so the audience shares his paranoia and his misreading of every clue.
Violence and war trauma: the Dachau flashbacks tie Andrew's personal grief to the wider violence of the 20th century.
Treatment versus surgery: Cawley's role-play is set against the 1950s rise of lobotomy and drugs, raising the question of what it means to cure a mind.
Identity as a choice: the last line asks whether a person can choose which version of himself to be, even at the cost of his self.
Runtime: 138 minutes. English-language, released in February 2010 after premiering at the Berlin International Film Festival.
Based on the 2003 novel Shutter Island by Dennis Lehane (also the author of Mystic River and Gone, Baby, Gone); the film follows the book closely but makes the ending more ambiguous.
Content: rated R in the US; includes the deaths of children, concentration-camp imagery and mental illness.
Rewatch value: many viewers rewatch it after the reveal, when the staff's odd reactions and small strange details read as deliberate clues.

faq.q: Was Teddy faking at the end of Shutter Island?
faq.a: The film does not say. The line about living as a monster or dying as a good man suggests he may be lucid and choosing the lobotomy, while novelist Dennis Lehane has said he reads it as a brief flash of sanity in a relapse.

faq.q: What does 'the law of 4' and 'who is 67' mean?
faq.a: They are clues Andrew wrote for himself. The four names Edward Daniels, Rachel Solando, Andrew Laeddis and Dolores Chanal pair up as anagrams, and the 67th patient is Andrew himself.

faq.q: Is Shutter Island a real place?
faq.a: No. Ashecliffe Hospital and Shutter Island are fictional, invented by Dennis Lehane for the novel, although the story is set in the real Boston Harbor.
